title: Interleaved request context fragmentation analysis
summary: Working notes from profiling sessions that reproduce a class of performance degradations when short (<=512 tokens) and long (>=16k tokens) requests are interleaved on a shared GPU pool. Observed across Llama-2-70B (fp16), Mistral-7B (qt8), Qwen-14B (fp16), and a small internal MoE variant (qwen-moe-32e). Root causes appear to be a combination of KV-cache fragmentation, expert-hotset churn, and allocator-induced kernel launch jitter.
background: We onboarded long-context endpoints (24k-32k) to the same serving clusters used for normal short-chat traffic. Early rollouts reported tail-latency regressions and occasional OOMs. Hypothesis space: (1) KV cache eviction/rewarm costs when prefixes are large and sparsely reused, (2) MoE expert allocation and load-balancing cost when requests have different routing footprints, (3) GPU memory allocator fragmentation and cudaMalloc/cudaFree noise during mixed workloads.
experiment_setup: Cluster: 8xA100-80GB per serving node. Runtime: redwood-serving v2.8. Models tested: llama-2-70b-fp16, mistral-7b-qt8, qwen-14b-fp16, qwen-moe-32e-qt8. Workloads: A) baseline uniform short requests (384 tokens). B) baseline uniform long requests (20k tokens). C) interleaved schedule: 10 short requests, 1 long, repeating; plus random jitter variant. Concurrency: 64 threads; request arrival Poisson. Batching policy: adaptive with 50ms cap. KV cache size limit: 40GB per GPU. MoE gating: standard softmax gating with top-2 experts. Measurements: p50/p90/p99 latency, tokens/sec, GPU memory high-water mark, kernel launch rate, allocator failure count.
profiling_commands:
nvprof --profile-from-start off -o profile.nvvp <run>
nsys profile --stats=true -o nsys-report <run>
python -m torch.profiler --schedule=(1,1) ...
heaptrack -- <binary>
rdma/pmem tracing via bpftrace scripts (link in linked_artifacts)
key_observations:
1) Interleaved schedule p99 latency increased by 2.7x vs short-only baseline; throughput dropped ~18%.
2) Long-only baseline had predictable higher latency but stable throughput.
3) GPU memory HWM climbed transiently during long request completion then slowly reclaimed; allocator showed many small cudaFree/cudaMalloc pairs when short requests followed a long request.
4) KV cache thrashing: long requests pin large prefix KV slices; short requests cause small partial cache writes that trigger eviction heuristics due to our shard-aware bucketization.
5) MoE model (qwen-moe-32e) showed expert-hotset churn: a long request routes to ~18 experts at different positions than short requests, causing migration of expert state between kernel launches and increased synchronization stalls.
6) Kernel trace shows bursts of micro-kernel launches (attention + rotary + softmax) interleaved with long GEMMs; launch latency variability correlates with allocator activity.
numeric_metrics:
short-only (llama-70b): p99=210ms, tps=120
long-only (llama-70b 20k): p99=4.1s, tps=8
interleaved (mixed): p99=560ms, tps=98
memory delta (interleaved vs short-only): +1.9GB avg HWM
allocator calls: +27% cudaMalloc events during interleaved runs
moe expert migration count per long request: median 12, 95th 22
hypotheses:
H1: KV cache bucketization is too coarse-grained for mixed-length workloads — long prefixes monopolize buckets and eviction heuristics thrash small writes.
H2: MoE routing produces non-overlapping expert activation patterns for long vs short requests; runtime migrates expert buffers and causes synchronization overhead.
H3: Our memory allocator (jemalloc/cuda pool) fragments under alternating large and small allocations leading to increased synchronous cudaMallocs and kernel launch jitter.
H4: Batching policy is amplifying the problem by trying to coalesce short requests during long-request processing and then flushing partially-filled batches.
mitigation_recommendations:
1) Context-length aware scheduling: mark requests by expected context length and place long requests on separate GPU pools (or isolated queues) to avoid cache and memory interference.
2) Rework KV cache bucketization: use adaptive bucket sizes based on prefix occupancy and maintain LRU at sub-bucket granularity to avoid evicting small-prefix entries when large prefixes are active.
3) MoE sticky-expert affinity: maintain per-client (or per-session) expert affinity maps and pre-allocate expert buffers to reduce migration churn when similar long/short requests reappear.
4) Pre-warm path for long requests: precommit large KV slices and reserve allocator slabs before execution to avoid synchronous cudaMallocs during critical path.
5) Batching policy: prefer latency-mode for short requests (no coalescing across long-request boundaries) and throughput-mode for long requests; implement a soft barrier that prevents mixing in adaptive scheduler.
6) Tune allocator: increase slab size and reuse threshold for small allocations to reduce cudaMalloc frequency. Consider using memory pools per-stream to reduce contention.
7) Investigate a lightweight admission-control signal from runtime to load-balancer to steer long requests away from nodes currently serving many short requests.
next_steps:
- Implement a short/long request tagging header and add routing rule in serving-proxy (P0)
- Prototype adaptive KV sub-bucket LRU (P1) and measure eviction rate change
- Add sticky-expert caching in qwen-moe runtime (experiment-only toggle)
- Run A/B on a canary pool with isolated long-request nodes for 2 weeks and collect p99, tps, OOM counts
- File follow-up GH PRs for allocator tuning knobs and a JIRA epic to track rollout
notes: Anecdotal: customers with heavy multi-turn transcripts saw higher error rates when bursts of background short-chat traffic occurred. This aligns with the eviction/rewarm cost hypothesis. Also seen small but measurable increase in API error 429 spikes due to queueing when interleaving is uncontrolled. Keep experiments reproducible: script to replay arrival patterns is checked into GH linked_artifacts.
